word-counter.what: Counts the words in your text instantly, including how it treats contractions, hyphenated words and apostrophes.
word-counter.howto: Paste or type your text into the box. The word and character counts update live, so you can trim to a target length as you write. Use it to hit a publication's word limit, a blog post length, or a word-count goal for a session.
word-counter.why: Word count is one of the few concrete, enforceable limits in writing. Editors and guidelines state a range; a word counter lets you meet it exactly instead of counting manually.

character-counter.what: Counts every character in your text, spaces and line breaks included, live as you type or paste.
character-counter.howto: Paste your text into the box and read the count as it updates. Use it against a hard limit: a meta description should stay under about 160 characters, a social post has its own ceiling, and many submission forms cut off silently after a set number.
character-counter.why: Character limits are everywhere in a writing life - headlines, captions, bios, pitch forms - and the fastest way to lose a submission is guessing. Ten seconds here beats a truncated form.
character-counter.know: Counts update live as you edit, so trimming to a limit is a process of watching the number, not repeated pasting. Line breaks count as characters in most form fields - if your text has hard wraps, remove them first for the honest figure.

character-counter-no-spaces.what: Counts characters the way some guidelines do - excluding spaces - so you can match a letters-only limit precisely.
character-counter-no-spaces.howto: Paste the text and compare the with-spaces and without-spaces counts. If a guideline says 2,000 characters excluding spaces, treat the lower number as your budget and trim until it fits with a few characters to spare.
character-counter-no-spaces.why: Space-inclusive and space-exclusive limits can differ by several percent on long text. Matching the number the editor actually meant saves a revise-and-resend.
character-counter-no-spaces.know: The gap between the two counts grows with every word - a 1,000-word draft typically carries 1,600-2,000 spaces. For long limits, check the no-spaces figure after every structural edit, not every sentence.

sentence-counter.what: Counts the sentences in your text by splitting on full stops, question marks and exclamation points, and reports the total live.
sentence-counter.howto: Paste a paragraph or a whole draft to see how many sentences you have. Read it next to the word count: the two together give your average sentence length, and anything above roughly 25 words per sentence on average is worth a second look.
sentence-counter.why: Sentence count is the quickest X-ray of rhythm. Thirty long sentences in a row read very differently from a deliberate mix, and editors feel the difference before they can name it.
sentence-counter.know: Ellipses, abbreviations like Dr. and decimal points can each fake a sentence break in mechanical counting - the number errs slightly high on abbreviation-heavy text, which is the safe direction for length limits.

paragraph-counter.what: Counts paragraphs - blocks of text separated by blank lines - so you can see a piece's structure at a glance.
paragraph-counter.howto: Paste the draft and check the count against its length. Online writing generally reads best with a paragraph every one to four sentences; a 1,000-word piece that counts three paragraphs is usually a sign to break it up.
paragraph-counter.why: Readers skim. Paragraph count is the shape of the skimming experience - a page that is one grey block loses readers a sentence after the headline.
paragraph-counter.know: Blank lines are what separate paragraphs here - a hard-wrapped pasted email can look like thirty paragraphs. Run line-break-cleaner first if the paste has wraps in odd places.

reading-time.what: Estimates how long a piece takes to read, from its word count at a typical silent-reading speed.
reading-time.howto: Paste the text to see the estimate. The usual assumption is roughly 200-250 words a minute; treat the figure as a band, not a promise - dense technical writing reads slower than a light list, and that is fine.
reading-time.why: Reading time is a promise made next to the headline. Estimating it honestly, and then delivering it, is a small trust signal that keeps readers coming back.
reading-time.know: The estimate assumes silent reading - reading aloud runs at roughly a third of the speed, so a five-minute read is closer to fifteen presented. Podcasters and video hosts: budget accordingly.

word-density.what: Shows your most frequent words and what share of the text each one is, so repetition and keyword-stuffing are visible at a glance.
word-density.howto: Paste the text and scan the top of the list. Function words like the and of will always lead; what matters is whether any content word - a name, a topic term, an adjective you lean on - appears far more than you intended.
word-density.why: Every writer has crutch words they cannot feel any more. Density is the objective mirror; cutting the echo makes prose read as crafted rather than looped.
word-density.know: Stopwords are not filtered, so the top of every list is the usual suspects - scroll past them. What counts as 'too high' depends on the word: a character's name at 2% is fine; an adjective at 2% is a tic.

case-converter.what: Converts text between UPPERCASE, lowercase, Title Case and Sentence case without retyping a word.
case-converter.howto: Paste the text, pick the target case, and copy the result. Title Case suits headlines and section titles; Sentence case is the safer default for subheadings in most house styles - check which one your publication uses and standardise.
case-converter.why: Retyping a paragraph to fix its capitalisation wastes minutes and introduces typos. A one-click conversion is exact, and exact is the point.
case-converter.know: Sentence case only fixes the first letter after each sentence end - proper nouns it cannot recognise stay lowercased, so give names and acronyms a final read. Title Case here follows simple style rules, not a specific manual.

text-cleaner.what: Normalises messy pasted text: non-breaking spaces become normal spaces, doubled spaces collapse, whitespace around line breaks disappears, and three or more blank lines collapse to one.
text-cleaner.howto: Paste text copied from emails, PDFs or web pages, then copy the cleaned version out. It is the fastest way to make imported text safe to edit - hidden non-breaking spaces are a classic cause of broken search and layout later.
text-cleaner.why: Text from the real world arrives dirty. Cleaning it first means every later step - counts, find-and-replace, formatting - works on what you think you wrote.
text-cleaner.know: The cleaner never changes your words - only spacing, blank lines and invisible characters. That makes it safe to run before you proofread: what you read afterwards is what a publisher will receive.

remove-extra-spaces.what: Collapses runs of spaces and tabs down to a single space while leaving your line breaks exactly where they are.
remove-extra-spaces.howto: Paste the text and copy the result. Use it on drafts assembled from messages and notes, where double spaces accumulate; paragraphs keep their shape and only the horizontal mess goes.
remove-extra-spaces.why: Double spaces survive every proofread done by eye. Collapsing them mechanically is faster and cannot miss one.
remove-extra-spaces.know: Tabs count as spaces here, which is usually what you want for prose. Code and tables are a different animal - indentation is meaningful there, so keep this tool away from it.

line-break-cleaner.what: Removes empty lines so wrapped paragraphs join cleanly - built for text pasted from PDFs and forms where blank lines multiply.
line-break-cleaner.howto: Paste the text and the tool strips the blank lines between wrapped lines; copy the result back into your editor. Run remove-extra-spaces first if the text also carries doubled spaces.
line-break-cleaner.why: A PDF paste with a blank line every forty characters is unusable in any editor. One pass here turns it back into prose you can actually work with.
line-break-cleaner.know: This removes empty lines only - the breaks inside paragraphs stay. For text where every line ends in a hard wrap with no blank lines, remove-extra-spaces plus a find-and-replace in your editor finishes the job.

text-sorter.what: Sorts the lines of your text alphabetically, ascending or descending, discarding empty lines.
text-sorter.howto: Put one item per line - names, references, list entries - paste, choose a direction, and copy the sorted result. It is the quick way to alphabetise a bibliography, a glossary or a contact list.
text-sorter.why: Editors notice an unsorted list. Sorting takes seconds and quietly signals that the details were handled.
text-sorter.know: Sorting is case-sensitive the way dictionaries are - capitalised entries sort before lowercase ones. Normalise the case first if your list mixes both and the order looks wrong.

duplicate-line-remover.what: Deletes repeated lines, keeping the first occurrence of each and preserving the original order.
duplicate-line-remover.howto: Paste your list - keywords, tags, citation lines - and copy the deduplicated result. Lines count as duplicates only when they match exactly after trimming, so near-duplicates still deserve your eye.
duplicate-line-remover.why: Duplicated lines in a list or a data set undermine trust in everything around them. Mechanical deduplication is exhaustive in a way scanning by eye never is.
duplicate-line-remover.know: Trailing spaces are trimmed before comparison, so 'item ' and 'item' count as one. Lines that differ by a single character or comma are not duplicates to the tool - scan the near-misses yourself.

writing-timer.what: A distraction-free session timer with a default 25-minute goal you can change, built for timed writing sprints.
writing-timer.howto: Set a goal in minutes, press start, and write in whatever document you like until it stops. A sprint works best with one rule: forward only - no editing until the timer ends.
writing-timer.why: Pages are written by sessions, not moods. A timer converts a vague intention into a bounded, repeatable block - which is the habit the whole craft rests on.
writing-timer.know: The timer keeps counting if you switch tabs, on purpose - the sprint is about time at the page, not words produced. Sessions of 15, 25 and 45 minutes all work; pick one and keep it boringly consistent.

article-outline-generator.what: Turns a topic and audience into a working outline skeleton - the point of the piece plus the moves that will prove it.
article-outline-generator.howto: Type your working title and who the piece is for, generate the outline, then edit it ruthlessly. Treat the result as a first argument to argue with, not a template to fill - the outline you disagree with teaches you what you actually think.
article-outline-generator.why: An outline written before drafting is the cheapest place to discover a piece does not work. Ten minutes here routinely saves a rewrite.
article-outline-generator.know: The strongest use is negative: generate an outline, find the section you cannot actually argue, and cut or research it. An outline that survives your own objections survives an editor's.

writing-checklist-generator.what: Builds a pre-submission checklist matched to the kind of piece you are sending - the checks an editor would run first.
writing-checklist-generator.howto: Pick the piece type, generate the checklist, and work down it during the final pass. Keep it open while you check; the point is catching what familiarity has made you blind to.
writing-checklist-generator.why: Most rejections on decent work are avoidable basics: the word count, the brief, the format. A checklist turns careful from a mood into a procedure.
writing-checklist-generator.know: Run the checklist before you format the submission, not after - fixing a structure problem at the formatting stage means doing the formatting twice.

syllable-counter.what: Counts syllables per word and across your text - the measurement behind every readability formula.
syllable-counter.howto: Paste text to see the total, or test single words to see how they score. English syllable counting is rule-based and occasionally surprised by odd spellings, so treat totals as close estimates rather than law.
syllable-counter.why: Syllable load is why utilise reads heavier than use. Seeing the number behind that feeling turns sentence-simplifying into a decision instead of an instinct.
syllable-counter.know: Rule-based counting trips on silent letters and borrowed words - fire is one syllable here, as it should be, but some proper nouns miscount. Use it for weights and trends, not single-word verdicts.

readability-score.what: Scores your text with the Flesch reading-ease formula - 0 to 100, higher is easier - and shows the words-per-sentence and syllables-per-word behind the score.
readability-score.howto: Paste a section and read the score with its grade band. General web writing sits comfortably around 60-70; if a piece lands far lower, look first at the longest sentences and the heaviest words.
readability-score.why: The score is not a verdict on intelligence - it is a measure of friction. Matching friction to your audience is what clear actually means.
readability-score.know: Score paragraphs, not whole documents - a 900-word piece mixing an intro and a technical section averages two different audiences into one misleading number.

filler-word-finder.what: Highlights filler words and hedges - the just, really, very and actually cushions that sneak into drafts.
filler-word-finder.howto: Paste a draft and work through the flagged words one by one. Do not delete blindly - sometimes the filler is doing tonal work. Cut it when the sentence survives without it, which is most of the time.
filler-word-finder.why: Filler is written in first drafts and forgotten by the second read. A mechanical list finds every one; your judgement decides which few earn their place.
filler-word-finder.know: Dialogue is exempt: characters say just and really the way people actually talk. Apply the edits to narration first and leave voices alone.

passive-voice-detector.what: Flags likely passive constructions - forms of to be with a past participle - so you can decide which ones to keep deliberately.
passive-voice-detector.howto: Paste the section and review each hit. Keep the passive when the actor is unknown or genuinely unimportant, as in the house was sold; rewrite when it hides who did what - mistakes were made is hiding someone.
passive-voice-detector.why: Passive voice is not a sin - reflexive passive voice is. Working from a list of candidates turns a style-guide slogan into sentence-level decisions.
passive-voice-detector.know: The detector flags patterns, not crimes - was and a participle sometimes form a perfectly active progressive (was running). Read each hit in its sentence before reaching for a rewrite.

word-repetition-checker.what: Finds your repeated content words - the ones a reader starts to notice by the third appearance.
word-repetition-checker.howto: Paste a section and look past the obvious function words at the top of the list. When a distinctive noun or verb repeats within a few paragraphs, keep one instance and vary or cut the rest - distance alone usually fixes it.
word-repetition-checker.why: Repetition is the tell of an unedited draft. Cutting echoes is the fastest single way to make prose feel professionally handled.
word-repetition-checker.know: Repetition across a gap of ten paragraphs is invisible to readers; repetition inside two is what they feel. Judge each repeat by its distance, not just its count.

sentence-length-checker.what: Measures every sentence in your text and shows the lengths, so you can see the rhythm - or the monotony - directly.
sentence-length-checker.howto: Paste a few paragraphs and look at the pattern of numbers. A run of similar lengths flattens the read; follow a long sentence with a short one and the page suddenly has pace.
sentence-length-checker.why: Readers hear sentence length before they notice anything else about style. Seeing the numbers lets you compose rhythm on purpose instead of by accident.
sentence-length-checker.know: Aim for variety, not shortness - a 30-word sentence followed by a 6-word one lands harder than twenty medium sentences. The pattern of numbers is the signal; the average is almost meaningless.

cliche-detector.what: Flags common cliches and worn phrases - the expressions readers skip because they have met them a thousand times.
cliche-detector.howto: Paste the draft and judge each flag: replace the phrase with what you actually mean, or keep it where the cliche is doing deliberate work, usually in dialogue or a joke.
cliche-detector.why: Cliches arrive pre-faded. A mechanical sweep finds the ones your own reading eye has gone blind to - which is all of them, eventually.
cliche-detector.know: The list covers the well-worn phrases, not fresh ones - your own pet phrase will not be flagged because nobody else has worn it out yet. Word-repetition-checker is the tool for that.

adverb-finder.what: Lists the adverbs in your text, led by the -ly words that most often mark an unnecessary one.
adverb-finder.howto: Paste the section and test each adverb: if the verb is right, the adverb is usually decoration - ran quickly is asking to be sprinted. Keep the ones that change the meaning; cut the ones that only add breath.
adverb-finder.why: Adverbs are how first drafts hedge. The verb-plus-adverb pair almost always hides a stronger verb, and finding it upgrades the whole sentence.
adverb-finder.know: Dialogue tags are the classic exception - she said quietly carries information that sprinted cannot. Fix the narration; let people talk the way they talk.

title-generator.what: Generates working title options from your topic, shaped for the kind of piece you are writing.
title-generator.howto: Enter the subject and the audience, generate, and treat every option as a draft - steal the structure, not the wording. A good title names the promise; test yours against the piece's actual first paragraph.
title-generator.why: Titles written at the last minute default to clever or vague. A batch of options gets you to specific - and specific is what makes a reader click or an editor read on.
title-generator.know: Generate twice with slightly different topic wording - the second batch is usually better because you will have sharpened what you are actually promising.

meta-description-generator.what: Drafts search-engine meta descriptions for a page, with the length discipline that keeps them from being truncated in results.
meta-description-generator.howto: Enter the page's subject and audience, generate, then edit so the description names what the page actually delivers. Keep it under roughly 160 characters and front-load the specific promise.
meta-description-generator.why: The meta description is your advert in the search results. Written deliberately it earns the click; left to auto-generation it reads like a receipt.
meta-description-generator.know: Write the description after the page is finished - the promise it makes has to be one the page keeps, and kept promises are what turn a visitor into a returning reader.

random-writing-prompt.what: Serves a random writing prompt whenever you need a starting line, a warm-up or a way out of a blank page.
random-writing-prompt.howto: Take the prompt and write against it for a fixed session - ten minutes, no stopping, no editing. The point is not the output; it is proof that you can start, which is the muscle everything else uses.
random-writing-prompt.why: Waiting for a good idea is a slow way to write. A prompt removes the decision and leaves only the writing - which is usually where the good idea was hiding.
random-writing-prompt.know: If a prompt leaves you cold, take its second word and change it - modifying the prompt is itself a writing decision, and the session starts the moment you make it.

word-document-converter.what: Converts between document formats in your browser - turning a .docx into clean text, or text into a document, without a word processor.
word-document-converter.howto: Choose the file, pick the output you need, and download the result. Formatting does not survive perfectly by design: you get the words and structure, not the fonts - which is what most submission guidelines actually ask for.
word-document-converter.why: Publications ask for formats; writers have files. A local conversion closes the gap without your draft ever leaving your machine.
word-document-converter.know: After converting, spot-check the start, the middle and the end - conversion is faithful to text and structure, but a thirty-second skim confirms nothing was dropped at a page boundary.

pdf-editor.what: Lets you edit a PDF's pages — rotate, delete, reorder — entirely in your browser.
pdf-editor.howto: Open a PDF, then use the controls on each page to rotate, remove or move it. Export a new PDF when you're happy. Nothing is uploaded.
pdf-editor.why: A quick fix to a PDF — a rotated scan, a page to drop — shouldn't need uploads or an account. Doing it client-side keeps it private.

pdf-to-text.what: Extracts plain text from a PDF so you can copy, quote and edit it. Runs entirely in your browser - the file is never uploaded.
pdf-to-text.howto: Choose the PDF and the text appears in the box, ready to copy. Scanned pages without a text layer come out empty - that is a property of the file, not a failure; those need optical recognition instead.
pdf-to-text.why: Quotes, guidelines and contracts arrive as PDFs. Getting them into editable text is the first step of working with any of them accurately.
pdf-to-text.know: Text comes out in the PDF's internal reading order - for two-column layouts that can interleave columns, so reflow the result before quoting line-by-line.

text-to-pdf.what: Turns plain text into a simple, clean PDF you can download - enough for a draft submission or a printable page.
text-to-pdf.howto: Paste the text, create the PDF, and open it to check. For formal submissions prefer the requester's stated format; this covers the times that just send a PDF is the whole requirement.
text-to-pdf.why: A PDF is a promise that the page will look the same on the editor's machine as on yours. Making one takes ten seconds here.
text-to-pdf.know: The PDF carries plain text only - no images, no signature line. For anything formal, add signatures and letterheads after downloading.

images-to-pdf.what: Combines JPG or PNG images into a single multi-page PDF, entirely in your browser.
images-to-pdf.howto: Add the images in order, build the PDF and download it. Scanned pages should be rotated and legible first - the tool binds what you give it; it does not clean up the scans.
images-to-pdf.why: Signed forms, markups and scanned documents travel best as one PDF. Binding them locally keeps private paperwork on your machine.
images-to-pdf.know: Page order follows the order you add images - add them in sequence or rebuild the PDF, because pages cannot be reordered inside the tool. Rotations should happen before the images arrive.

self-plagiarism-checker.what: Checks a text for repeated or near-identical sentences within itself - internal duplication, the accidental kind.
self-plagiarism-checker.howto: Paste the draft, run the check and read each repeated pair. Boilerplate you meant to repeat can stay; the accidental near-echoes two paragraphs apart are what an editor would find first.
self-plagiarism-checker.why: Nobody rereads 3,000 words hunting their own repeats. The tool does, exhaustively, in seconds - before a reader does it for you in a review.
self-plagiarism-checker.know: Run it on the full draft, not sections - the echoes it exists to catch are the ones separated by enough text that you forgot writing the first one.

ai-writing-checker.what: A rule-based heuristic that flags formulaic phrases and AI-favoured wording in your text - an honesty nudge, not a verdict.
ai-writing-checker.howto: Paste the text, analyse, and judge each flag. Where a flagged phrase does real work, keep it; where it is filler - in today's fast-paced world and friends - rewrite it in your own voice. No tool can reliably detect AI; this one detects the style.
ai-writing-checker.why: If you edit AI-drafted text, the risk is shipping generic prose under your name. This finds the generic so your voice can replace it.
ai-writing-checker.know: Treat every flag as a question, not an instruction - the goal is a draft that sounds like you, not a draft that avoids a word list. If a flagged phrase is genuinely yours, keep it without guilt.

tone-checker.what: Estimates whether a piece of writing reads as formal, neutral or conversational, and shows you which signals produced that estimate.
tone-checker.howto: Paste a paragraph or a whole draft. Read the band first — Formal, Neutral or Conversational — then look at the signal table to see what is driving it. If the score is higher than you want, add a few contractions and address the reader directly. If it is lower than you want, cut the exclamation marks, replace casual words, and use connectives like however and therefore to join ideas.
tone-checker.why: Most writing that fails does not fail on grammar; it fails because the register is wrong for the reader. A cover letter that sounds like a text message and an email to a friend that sounds like a contract both misfire. Tone is a deliberate choice, and it is much easier to adjust once you can see it.

citation-formatter.what: Assembles a single reference in APA, MLA or Chicago style from the details you enter.
citation-formatter.howto: Choose the style your institution or publication requires, then choose whether the source is a book, an article or a web page. Fill in what you have — author, title, container (the journal, website or newspaper), year, publisher and URL. The formatted reference updates as you type; copy it into your reference list.
citation-formatter.why: Citation style is a mechanical rule set, and losing marks to a misplaced full stop is a waste. Formatting one reference correctly also teaches you the pattern, so the next twenty are faster. Always check the result against your own style sheet: editions differ, and the version your marker uses is the one that counts.

word-alternatives.what: A curated set of the words and phrases that most often weaken writing, each with stronger replacements.
word-alternatives.howto: Type a single word or short phrase — said, very, good, thing, in order to — and BRYME shows alternatives. Where the honest advice is to delete the word rather than replace it, the tool says so. Use it while editing, not while drafting.
word-alternatives.why: This is deliberately not a full thesaurus. A general thesaurus encourages the worst habit in student writing: swapping a plain word for a longer one that does not quite mean the same thing. This list covers the handful of words that genuinely flatten a sentence, and it tells you when the plain word was right all along.

outline-builder.what: An interactive outline you can reorder and budget, rather than a fixed list generated once.
outline-builder.howto: Pick the kind of thing you are writing and BRYME loads a starting scaffold. Then argue with it: rename sections to say what yours actually does, delete the ones that do not apply, add your own, drag the order around with the arrows, and give each section a word target. The totals update as you go. Copy the outline into your document before you start drafting.
outline-builder.why: The scaffold is not the value — editing it is. A generic outline tells you nothing, but a generic outline you have deliberately changed forces you to decide what each section is for and roughly how much of the piece it deserves. Budgeting words per section is also the most reliable way to catch a structural problem early: if your introduction has been allocated a third of the piece, the plan is wrong and you have found out before writing 2,000 words.

freelance-rate-calculator.what: Arithmetic for the question every freelancer gets wrong: what do I actually have to charge?
freelance-rate-calculator.howto: Enter what you need to earn in a year after tax. Add your business expenses and your tax rate, then be honest about how many hours a week you can genuinely bill — for most freelance writers it is 15 to 25, not 40. The calculator grosses everything up and gives you an hourly, per-word and per-piece figure.
freelance-rate-calculator.why: Most writers price by copying whatever number they saw someone else quote, then discover they are working sixty hours to earn less than a salary. Two things cause it. First, tax and expenses come out before you get paid, so the invoice has to be larger than your target. Second, only a fraction of your week is billable — pitching, admin, invoicing and chasing late payment are real hours that no client pays for. Pricing as though every hour is billable is the single most common way freelance writers underprice themselves. This tool is arithmetic, not market data: check the result against the real stated rates on BRYME's opportunity listings before you quote anyone.

word-count-to-pages.what: Words to pages for a specific, stated format — not a vague average.
word-count-to-pages.howto: Enter your word count and pick the format the brief actually specifies. If you do not know the spec, use standard manuscript format, which is what most editors and agents mean. You also get read-aloud time, which is what you need for a speech or a video script.
word-count-to-pages.why: “Pages” is not a unit of length. The same 1,000 words is four double-spaced pages or two single-spaced ones, and a printed book page holds different amounts again depending on trim size. This causes real problems: a student told to write “five pages” and a writer told “1,250 words” are being asked for the same thing, but only one of those instructions is unambiguous. If a brief gives you a page count, ask which spec it means. If you are submitting work, state the word count — that is what editors work from.

invoice-generator.what: A fill-in-and-print invoice built for writing work: line items by project or word count, nine currency options matching the markets this site covers, automatic totals with optional tax, and a clean document you print or save as PDF.
invoice-generator.howto: Fill in your name and the client's details, add one line per piece of work (a feature, a content package, a day rate), and pick the currency you invoiced in. The totals compute as you type. Hit print and choose 'Save as PDF' to email it — or print it the old way. Your details stay saved on this device for next time.
invoice-generator.why: Invoices get paid faster when they look like they came from a business, not a favour. The guide to [invoicing as a writer](/learn/freelance-paid-writing/how-to-invoice-as-a-writer/) covers what to put on it; this tool handles what it looks like. Nothing is uploaded anywhere — your rates and clients are your business, literally.

freelance-agreement-builder.what: A plain-language freelance agreement for writing engagements: the parties, the scope, the fee and payment terms, revision rounds, a cancellation clause, rights transfer on payment, and governing law — as a printable document.
freelance-agreement-builder.howto: Fill in both parties, describe the project and the deliverables (one per line), set the fee and payment terms, and choose how many revision rounds are included. The agreement renders as you type. Print two copies, sign both, and each party keeps one. Save as PDF via the print dialog if you need to email it first.
freelance-agreement-builder.why: The guide to [writer contracts](/learn/freelance-paid-writing/writing-contracts-what-to-check/) explains what each clause is for; this tool turns those clauses into a document a small client can read and sign the same day. It is a general template — for high-value or unusual engagements, have a local professional review it. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

late-payment-letter-builder.what: Three escalating letters for an unpaid invoice — a polite reminder, a firm follow-up, and a final notice — generated from the same invoice details. Days overdue compute from the due date, the amount formats in your currency, and every letter names one clear next step.
late-payment-letter-builder.howto: Fill in what's on the invoice — who owes you, how much, when it fell due — then pick the stage you've reached. Start at stage one and wait a few working days before escalating. Read the preview, adjust anything in the form, then print the letter or copy its text straight into an email. Your details stay on this device.
late-payment-letter-builder.why: Chasing money you're owed is the most awkward fifteen minutes in freelancing — which is exactly why the guide to [invoicing a publication](/learn/freelance-paid-writing/how-to-invoice-as-a-writer/) says to chase on a schedule, in writing, with a set escalation path. A letter that states facts — amount, days overdue, one clear ask — reads as administration rather than aggression, and most clients pay long before stage three.

pitch-checker.what: Ten rule-based checks — the ones a commissioning editor runs in the first ten seconds: length, sentence load, evidence of clips, the clear ask, filler, passive constructions, exclamation discipline — applied to your pasted pitch, each verdict with a one-line fix.
pitch-checker.howto: Paste your pitch, add the subject line and the publication's name, and press check. Green passes, amber is a note, red means fix before sending. Adjust, re-check, send.
pitch-checker.why: Most pitches die on rules no editor states: too long, no clips, no ask, a hedged voice. The guide to [how to write a pitch](/guides/how-to-write-a-pitch/) teaches the structure; this tool is the ten-second edit before you hit send. It is deliberately rule-based rather than generative — no AI writes for you, because a pitch must be in your voice and because publications increasingly reject machine-written submissions.

tax-estimator.what: It turns one number writers avoid - what do I owe? - into a plan: your taxable base after deductible expenses, the total to set aside at your chosen rate, the per-quarter amount if you pay quarterly, and what actually stays yours.
tax-estimator.howto: Enter what clients will pay you this year, your deductible business expenses, a set-aside percentage (25% is a common starting point) and anything you have already put away. Update it whenever a big payment lands.
tax-estimator.why: Freelance income arrives gross - no employer withheld anything. The writers who get hurt are not the ones who owe tax; they are the ones who spent it. A fixed set-aside rate, applied the moment payment lands, removes the cliff entirely.

income-tracker.what: A private running ledger for your writing money: log every payment, invoice and pending fee, and it keeps the year's total, this month, your average per piece, and which clients actually pay (and how much of your income depends on each).
income-tracker.howto: After any payment lands - or you send an invoice - add the client, amount, date and status. Export to CSV whenever you want a backup or your accountant's favourite file. Everything stays in your browser; nothing is uploaded.
income-tracker.why: Writers who track every payment spot the patterns that change businesses: which client is quietly becoming 60% of your income, which months run thin, and exactly how much to set aside before tax. What gets measured gets negotiated.

structure-quiz.what: Eight multiple-choice questions on the mechanics that hold writing together: the lede's real job, the inverted pyramid, the nut graf, three-act structure, show-don't-tell, skimmability, the through-line of meaning, and how professionals start a long piece.
structure-quiz.howto: Pick an answer for each question - you get the correct answer and a one-line why immediately. Eight questions, about two minutes. Your score comes with a straight verdict, and Try again reruns the ones you missed.
structure-quiz.why: Most writing problems are structure problems wearing a disguise. A piece that 'doesn't flow' usually has an unkept promise in its opening or moves that arrive in the wrong order. Name the mechanics and they become tools instead of luck.

deadline-tracker.what: A private deadline list for pitches and commissions, stored in this browser only - nothing is uploaded to any server.
deadline-tracker.howto: Add each commission with its due date and check the list as work lands. Storage is local to this browser: clearing site data clears the list, so export anything you cannot afford to lose.
deadline-tracker.why: Missed deadlines end client relationships faster than bad prose does. A list you will actually look at - because it takes one click - is the system that survives busy weeks.
deadline-tracker.know: Add the internal deadline a day before the real one - the tracker records what you tell it, and a one-day buffer converts near-misses into on-time deliveries.
